questions.q: Define situational irony and give one example from daily life (not from the story).
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when the outcome of a situation is sharply contrary to what was expected or intended. Example: A fire station burning down while firefighters are out on a call. A wrong answer (e.g., "irony is just a coincidence" or "irony is when something funny happens") reveals the student conflates irony with mere surprise or humour, missing the structural contradiction between expectation and result that defines the device.

questions.q: In "Udd ka Naksha," Vyasingh frames Eka Okha to secure him a government job. Explain why this is situational irony, not just a plot twist.
questions.a: It is situational irony because Vyasingh's corrupt act (framing an innocent man) produces the opposite of its intended harm: it grants Eka Okha the secure livelihood and dignity that the "honest" system denied him. The outcome — a poor man's salvation through a crook's scheme — inverts the moral expectation that virtue rewards virtue. A wrong answer (e.g., "it's ironic because Vyasingh is bad") shows the student identifies character contrast but misses the structural reversal of intended vs. actual consequence.

questions.q: Identify the central symbol in the story's title "Udd ka Naksha" and explain what abstract concept it represents, using one textual detail.
questions.a: The "map of the heart" (udd ka naksha) symbolises moral orientation — the inner compass that guides choices between conscience and compromise. Textual detail: The story ends with Eka Okha literally holding a survey map while having proven his loyalty to truth over tenure, making the physical map a metaphor for his ethical bearings. A wrong answer (e.g., "it's just a map of the village") treats the symbol as literal setting, ignoring the abstraction (heart = conscience, map = guidance) that the title establishes.

questions.q: Compare the dramatic irony in the scene where the British officer praises Vyasingh's "loyalty" with the verbal irony in Eka Okha's final refusal of the job. How do they target different aspects of colonial power?
questions.a: Dramatic irony: the officer (and reader) knows Vyasingh manipulated the system, but the officer praises him as a model servant — exposing colonial bureaucracy's blindness to its own corruption. Verbal irony: Eka Okha says "I don't need your favour" while accepting the dignity the job offered — his words reject the patronage, but his act claims the self-respect the system tried to buy. Together, they dismantle colonial authority from both ends: the ruler's ignorance and the subject's resistance. A wrong answer that merely lists the two scenes without contrasting their targets (institutional blindness vs. individual agency) shows fragmented analysis.

questions.q: Evaluate: Is the story's ending — Eka Okha unemployed but morally intact — a symbolic victory or a practical defeat? Defend your judgment with two pieces of evidence.
questions.a: It is a symbolic victory. Evidence 1: Eka Okha returns the appointment letter, choosing poverty over complicity, making his empty hands a symbol of uncompromised conscience. Evidence 2: The final image of him walking away "with his head high" (sir uncha karke) transforms material loss into moral stature, aligning with the title's "map of the heart" — he has navigated correctly. A response calling it "defeat because he lost the job" prioritises plot outcome over thematic resolution, missing how Premchand uses symbolism to redefine victory in a colonised society.

questions.q: Write a 4-line paragraph using verbal irony to describe a modern situation where a corrupt official is honoured for "transparency." Do not name the device explicitly.
questions.a: The anti-corruption award glittered in his palms, polished by the very files he buried. "A beacon of integrity," the citation read, while his locker swallowed another crore. The audience clapped louder, grateful for such rare honesty. He smiled, knowing the best hideouts are built on applause. A poor answer would state the irony directly ("It is ironic that...") or write a sincere description, showing the student cannot wield the device — only recognise it.
